newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FEATURE - "Think for yourselves," Singapore says.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - "Think for yourselves," Singapore says.

text.p: Behind neat rows of traditional school desks, Denise James's English literature class waits quietly for the lesson to begin.

Dressed in clean, white shirts, shorts and plimsolls with neat, brushed hair, the 40 pupils look like any other class of respectful Chinese 13-year-olds in this prosperous and orderly Southeast Asian city-state.

But James's class is part of an experiment that is trying to overturn traditional Asian methods of teaching and encourage children to do what until recently would have been unheard of: think creatively and question authority.

The Singapore government has committed Singapore $2.5 billion (US$1.74 billion) to a plan to revolutionise Singapore teaching methods by introducing innovative thinking into classrooms and improving the handling of information technology.
"We are trying to get children to think for themselves, to be more creative, productive," said James.

As her class begins, the differences appear. Once the topic for the lesson is introduced -- time travel -- the pupils turn away from the traditional blackboard and break into smaller groups that begin lively discussions of the set story.

James encourages them to question the different concepts used in the story, such as time, and then think how the same concepts could be applied to everyday life. The pupils suggest their own innovative ways of solving everyday problems.
Chua-Lim Yen Ching, the principal of Zhonghua Secondary School, one of five schools running the experiment, says Singapore students need to learn to be more innovative.
SINGAPORE STUDENTS DILIGENT BUT NEED HAND-HOLDING

Singapore schools have an enviable reputation. Last year the sland dominated the 41-nation International Maths and Science Study, surpassing schools from Japan and Germany. The World Competitiveness Yearbook 1996 rated the island's education system number one in meeting the needs of a competitive economy.

But employers say that although Singapore school-leavers and graduates are competent and diligent and have good analytical abilities, they need lots of hand-holding, have problems working independently and have difficulty thinking creatively.
Desmond Supple, economist at BZW in Singapore, says these skills are essential as Singapore graduates from "developing" status to a "developed" economy at the cutting edge of industry.
"As Singapore's economy matures, it is moving into higher value-added production such as research and development, computers and financial services," said Supple.
"In these kind of industries, productivity gains depend on individual innovation and enterprise," he said. "That is where the individual creative talent is at a premium."
This is quite a challenge for Singapore, which has been organised centrally by one dominant force for almost 40 years.

In that time, the ruling People's Action Party (PAP), first under the charismatic leadership of Lee Kuan Yew and now under Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong, has held a tight rein on the media and used hardball tactics to keep opposition to a minimum.
Critics say the PAP's domination of almost all aspects of life in Singapore has stifled innovation and free-thinking.
But Rebecca Moc, a deputy director in Singapore's Ministry of Education, says free-thinking is now more encouraged.
"Whereas the old hierarchical structure worked very well -- it was a pyramid with the people at the top doing the thinking for the rest -- it may not work well in future," she said.
"It would be better to have all members of the workforce able to ask questions, to solve problems in their own areas of work: creativity and innovation in the workplace at all levels."
CULTURAL INHIBITIONS

Lim Pin, vice chancellor of The National University of Singapore, says the computer revolution is forcing a change in attitude. With the information technology explosion, it is more important to learn how to select information than accumulate it.

To encourage creative thinking in higher education, Lim and his colleagues are making examinations more course-based and introducing "open book" exams that test students' ability to sort and evaluate information rather than memorise it.
But he says many Singaporeans have been inhibited from thinking creatively by cultural factors.
"Singaporean students are by and large very shy, not assertive, and I believe that they are culturally reticent," he said. "We need to encourage this latent capability to speak up."
